description: Team Tesis is a group of Computer Engineering students at Universidad Católica del Uruguay (UCU). We took part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge to apply our training to a real scientific problem using open data from NASA and other space agencies. The search for Earth analogs of the Moon and Mars interested us because it combines data engineering, geospatial analysis and software design with a question relevant to future exploration.
summary:
Earth Connect is a web platform that systematically searches Earth for candidate analogs of scientifically interesting locations on the Moon and Mars. Starting from a target point on the Moon or Mars, users select variables such as elevation, slope, local relief and surface temperature, set hard constraints and add weights if needed. The system returns a ranked list of Earth locations on an interactive map and table. It computes multi-variable similarity and explains it, so every result shows how much each variable contributes to the score, how comparable it is between bodies and where the analogy breaks down.
Searches are reproducible and the form generates visible SQL on DuckDB that researchers can open, edit and re-run.
As future work, a machine-learning module will go further by modeling how terrain and surface conditions change over time, which will make it possible to predict which locations that do not match today are likely to resemble the target site in the future. The platform is built on open NASA data and other datasets. The MVP indexes 25 environmental and quality fields on a nominal 4 × 4 km global grid, with a broader catalog of 91 candidate variables for future expansion.
By making analog discovery systematic, explainable and reproducible, Terra Analog Finder helps mission teams look beyond the few well-known sites and choose the right place for each test.
details:
Earth Connect is a full-stack web application that turns the search for planetary analogs into a systematic, data-driven process. Its core is a deterministic search. The user starts by choosing the Moon or Mars and picking a target point, either by clicking on the map or by entering its coordinates. The platform shows the values of each variable at that point and lets the user choose which ones to compare, such as elevation, slope, local relief, topographic position and day and night surface temperature. Each criterion can be marked as mandatory, which filters out any candidate that does not meet it, or as optional, in which case it receives a weight and contributes to a similarity score. The system then ranks Earth locations by that score and displays the best candidates on an interactive map and in a sortable table. For every candidate it shows a breakdown of how much each variable contributed, so the user can see why a place ranks where it does and where the analogy breaks down. Nothing in this search is estimated. The ranking comes from reference data and explicit rules, so the same search always returns the same result.

The next stage, which is future work, will add the assessments of a machine-learning model and keep them separate from the deterministic ranking. The model will look at how terrain and surface conditions change over time and estimate which locations that do not match the target today are likely to resemble it in the future. These assessments will be predictions rather than measurements, so the platform will present them as a complement to the search results and will not mix them into the similarity score.

The main benefit is transparency. The search form generates visible SQL that advanced users can open, edit and run again in a read-only console, and the same search on the same version of the data always returns the same result. Once the prediction module is in place, it will add foresight by giving researchers an early view of sites worth monitoring. The intended impact is to help scientists and mission teams look beyond the small group of well-known analog sites, compare candidates across the whole planet with the same criteria, and choose the right place to test instruments, rovers and operations before they fly.

We built the project with Python for data processing, a Rust backend with Axum and Tonic, DuckDB for storage and queries, and TypeScript with React, MapLibre and deck.gl for the interface. The data comes from open NASA products such as MODIS and POWER and from other open datasets, while Moon and Mars values are sampled on demand from NASA Trek and ASU/JMARS services. The MVP indexes 25 environmental and quality fields on a nominal 4 × 4 km global grid, with a broader catalog of 91 candidate variables for future expansion.
